title: County of Vexin
capsule: The Vexin was a disputed county straddling the boundary between the Île-de-France and Normandy — divided into the French Vexin west of the Epte river and the Norman Vexin east of it by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911) — whose possession became acutely contested after William the Conqueror's 1066 assumption of the English crown made a single magnate sovereign over both neighboring powers. The county was held in the later eleventh century by Gauthier III and then Count Simon de Vexin, whose entry into a monastery in 1077 extinguished the comital line and triggered French seizure. Philip I of France incorporated the French Vexin in 1082; William the Conqueror's retaliatory raid on the French Vexin in 1087 resulted in the wound from which he died at Rouen that September. The Norman Vexin subsequently passed through the hands of successive Norman and Angevin kings of England before being ceded to France under the Treaty of Le Goulet (1200).
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The geographic division of the Vexin is well-documented in medieval sources; the precise county boundaries within the 990–1085 window are established from charter evidence, though the split between French and Norman Vexin complicates any single polygon representation.
